title: DNF versus d-DNNF succinctness
formal: Is the following nonuniform size separation true? For every \(C\geq1\), integer \(k\geq1\) and \(N\geq1\), there is a DNF formula \(F\) of size \(s\geq N\) such that every d-DNNF circuit computing exactly the same Boolean function on the same input variables has size greater than \(C(s+1)^{k}\). Equivalently, is there no single polynomial bound on the size of a d-DNNF representation of an arbitrary DNF? No efficient construction or conversion algorithm is required on either side of this size comparison.
why: The question measures an inherent space cost of making overlapping explanations disjoint while retaining decomposable structure. It determines whether the simplest compact disjunctive representation can always remain compact in a form suited to exact counting, independently of how difficult that form is to find.

importance.reason: Determines the representation-size cost of determinism when compiling knowledge into a form supporting exact model counting.

category_assignment.reason: The main target is Boolean representation size, succinctness or a separation between circuit/encoding languages.

sentences: A DNF formula describes satisfying assignments as a union of conjunctions, whose cases may overlap.
The proposal asks whether some polynomial-size DNFs require superpolynomial-size deterministic decomposable circuits for the same Boolean function.
Determinism requires disjoint alternatives, while decomposability requires conjunctions to separate their variables.
A separation would show that imposing these useful structural restrictions can force an inherent representation-size increase.

The question is about the existence of compact equivalent circuits, so hardness of efficiently finding a conversion or a separation for unrestricted DNNFs does not by itself answer this more specific size comparison.

definitions: Inputs are Boolean variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\). A DNF is a finite disjunction of terms, each a conjunction of distinct literals with no contradictory pair; the empty conjunction is true and the empty disjunction false. Its size is one plus its number of terms and literal occurrences. An NNF circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output, leaves labeled by literals or the constants zero and one, and internal AND and OR gates of arbitrary finite fan-in. It may share subcircuits and have unrestricted depth. Its size is its total number of vertices and edges. The variable set of a gate comprises variables labeling leaves that reach it. Decomposability means that the variable sets of different children of every AND gate are pairwise disjoint. Determinism means that, for every OR gate and every assignment to the union of its children’s variable sets, at most one child evaluates to one. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions. Equivalent circuits agree for every input assignment, with no error or auxiliary existentially quantified variables. There is no common variable order, tree-structured decomposition, restriction to decision gates, or uniformity requirement. Polynomial comparisons use the DNF representation size, including all literal occurrences; ordinary explicit gate/edge encodings give the same polynomial-versus-superpolynomial distinction. The family formulation using polynomial-size DNFs in the number of inputs is equivalent after permitting unused input variables as padding.

context_blocks.text: Decomposability separates the variable sets of conjunctions, while determinism makes the alternatives at each disjunction disjoint. These restrictions support exact model counting in time polynomial in the representation size. A DNF already satisfies decomposability after inconsistent terms are removed, but its terms need not be disjoint.

Capelli’s June 2026 habilitation explicitly asks for a superpolynomial d-DNNF lower bound for DNF formulas. The known separation of unrestricted DNNF from d-DNNF uses a broader source representation and therefore does not settle this DNF restriction.

Even if every DNF has a polynomial-size d-DNNF representation, finding one in polynomial time would have additional counting consequences. The source distinguishes this algorithmic conversion issue from the existence of small representations; conditional conversion hardness supplies no unconditional size separation.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified superpolynomial size separation, or refute it by proving that one polynomial bounds the minimum equivalent d-DNNF size for every DNF. A negative answer need not give an efficient converter. A lower bound for decision-DNNF, structured d-DNNF, or a broader DNNF input family does not meet the stated unrestricted-output, DNF-input criterion.
